title: Keeping the Church’s history became a calling, not a favor
setting: This short revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, around 8 March 1831. John Whitmer had already served as a scribe for Joseph Smith. He was asked to keep a history, but he said he would rather not. He agreed to serve if the Lord made his will known through Joseph. Joseph then dictated this revelation, and Whitmer accepted. One later copy dates it 7 March.
summary: The revelation names John Whitmer to write and keep a regular history. He is also to help Joseph Smith copy all that is revealed. He may speak in meetings when it is fitting. He is to keep the church record and history continually. The reason given is that Oliver Cowdery has another office. If John is faithful, the Comforter will help him write.

contextNote.title: A record kept by assignment
contextNote.text: John Whitmer did not want the job of historian. Verse 1 settles the question by naming him to keep “a regular history”. Verse 3 gives the practical reason: Oliver Cowdery had been appointed to another office. Verse 4 then ties the work to faithfulness and the Comforter’s help. So the history is framed as spiritual work, not only clerical work. In this passage, a “regular” history is a steady, ongoing record kept by calling.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 46–48 draws from this revelation the value of keeping records. According to verse 4, what would help John Whitmer write, and how might that apply to your own record keeping?
reviewNote: Read all 4 verses. Official heading gives Kirtland, 8 March 1831, to John Whitmer, with his reluctance. JSP dates it circa 8 March; Revelation Book 2 gives 7 March and the Book of Commandments only March 1831. JSP says record keeping had been sporadic before, and Whitmer later compiled Revelation Book 1 and a history. Fact-check 2026-10-12: no changes
